title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch from Jira to Plane to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to host their own data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively straightforward to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane uses a third-party plugin for Git integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550.00-$2,900.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
	+ Robust feature set
	+ Native integration with Git
	+ Scalable for large teams
	+ Mobile app available
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Data stored on Jira's servers
	+ Complex setup process
**Plane:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and self-hosted
	+ Simple setup process
	+ Data ownership and control
	+ Customizable
* Cons:
	+ Limited scalability
	+ No native integration with Git
	+ Limited mobile support
	+ May require technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams and enterprises that need a robust feature set and native integration with Git. It is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem and want to take advantage of Jira's scalability. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want a simple, self-hosted project management tool with data ownership and control. It is also a good choice for teams that are on a tight budget and want to avoid per-user fees.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a new Plane instance and configure the necessary plugins and integrations.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Test and verify that all data has been imported correctly.
5. Update any custom workflows or scripts to work with Plane's API.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's Git integration is currently provided by a third-party plugin, which may not be as robust as Jira's native integration. However, for small to medium-sized teams that want a simple, self-hosted project management tool with data ownership and control, Plane is a good choice and may be worth considering.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need native Git integration
* Teams on a tight budget that want to avoid per-user fees
* Teams that value data ownership and control
* Teams with simple project management needs
* Teams that are already self-hosting other tools and want to add a project management tool to their stack

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted. However, you will need to pay for server costs if you choose to self-host.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Does Plane have native integration with Git?
No, Plane's Git integration is currently provided by a third-party plugin.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is currently better suited for small to medium-sized teams due to its limited scalability.
### Can I use Plane on mobile devices?
Yes, but mobile support is currently limited and may not be as robust as Jira's mobile app.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

The core use case for both tools is project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Linear offers a free plan and a paid plan at $8/user/month, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full ownership of their data since it's self-hosted, whereas Linear stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, whereas Linear is easier to set up.
* Scalability: Linear is more scalable and can handle larger teams, whereas Plane's scalability depends on the server it's hosted on.
* Integration: Linear has a more comprehensive integration with third-party tools, whereas Plane has limited integrations but allows for custom integrations through its API.

| Aspect | Linear | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $8/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,600/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Linear
* Easy to set up and use
* Comprehensive integration with third-party tools
* Scalable and can handle large teams
* Offers a free plan
* Limited control over data
### Plane
* Self-hosted and free
* Full control over data
* Customizable through API
* Open-source and community-driven
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Linear is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and scalability. It's ideal for large teams that need a comprehensive project management tool with integrations with third-party tools. * Teams with technical expertise that want a self-hosted project management tool
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and control
* Teams that don't need a scalable project management tool

# Microsoft Teams vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Microsoft Teams and Mattermost are two popular communication and collaboration platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer a range of features, including chat, video conferencing, and file sharing, making them ideal for businesses, educational institutions, and community groups. The core use case for both tools is to facilitate teamwork and communication, and someone would switch from Microsoft Teams to Mattermost for reasons such as data ownership, cost savings, or the need for self-hosting.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Microsoft Teams offers a free version, as well as paid plans starting at $6 per user per month, while Mattermost is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows users to self-host and maintain full control over their data, whereas Microsoft Teams stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Microsoft Teams is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both tools can scale to meet the needs of large organizations, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility and control.
* Integration: Microsoft Teams integrates seamlessly with other Microsoft tools, such as Office 365, while Mattermost offers integrations with a wide range of third-party tools, including GitHub and Jira.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Microsoft Teams | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $6-$22/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $6-$22/user/month (approximately $300-$1,100/month) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $6-$22/user/month (approximately $1,200-$4,400/month) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Microsoft Teams:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Seamless integration with other Microsoft tools
* Robust feature set, including video conferencing and file sharing
* Large user community and extensive support resources
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosting option provides full control over data and security
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Free and open-source, with a low total cost of ownership

4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your Microsoft Teams setup, including channels, users, and permissions.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a high degree of customization and extensibility. title: Google Workspace vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
